title: Heading Broadcast Network Topology
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: Interactive Mermaid network diagram of a master robot that hosts a WiFi access point and sends UDP heading packets to many followers. A toolbar switches to Chapter 12's one-to-one BLE pairing and Chapter 11's router-hosted WiFi, and a Compare card shows what the sender must change when a follower is added.

educational.topic: UDP broadcast topology for heading synchronization
learningObjectives: Differentiate a one-to-many UDP broadcast topology from one-to-one BLE pairing and router-hosted WiFi.
Identify which device hosts the network in each topology.
Explain why adding a follower requires no change to a UDP broadcast master but does require a new BLE connection.
Explain why a dropped UDP heading packet is not a failure for a follower.
prerequisites: Station-mode WiFi and TCP web servers (Chapter 11)
WiFi access point host mode and UDP broadcast (Chapter 13)
standards: CSTA 3A-NI-04: Evaluate the scalability and reliability of networks, by describing the relationship between routers, switches, servers, topology, and addressing.

controls.label: Router WiFi
controls.purpose: Show Chapter 11's router-hosted network with TCP connections.

controls.label: Add Follower 4
controls.purpose: Add a fourth follower to the swarm views and update the Compare card.

userInterface.hoverTargets: Every node, every arrow and arrow label, and the dashed network outline show an explanation in the Details card on hover or click.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Contrasting cases: the same four comparison facts shown for three network topologies
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Topology switcher with hover/click explanations and a live comparison card
keyQuestions: Who hosts the network in each topology?
How many sends does the leader make per update with four followers in each topology?
What must change on the master to add a fifth follower?
commonMisconceptions: The master must send a separate packet to each follower (one broadcast packet reaches all of them).
A lost UDP packet breaks the swarm (the next heading packet arrives about 20 ms later).
All WiFi projects need a router (the Pico W can host its own access point).
assessmentOpportunities: Three-column comparison table of host, links, sends per update, and scaling cost.
Claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the best topology for a 10-robot swarm.
Exit ticket: list the master-side changes needed for a fifth follower.
